content.title: Meet The First Female Astronaut To Go On A Moon Mission
content.text: NASA astronaut Christina Koch reacts shortly after landing in Kazakhstan, on Feb. 6, 2020, having shattered the spaceflight record for female astronauts after almost a year aboard the International Space Station. (Photo by Sergei ILNITSKY / POOL / AFP) (Photo by SERGEI ILNITSKY/POOL/AFP via Getty Images)POOL/AFP via Getty ImagesWhen NASA launches its Artemis II mission, scheduled for this week, one astronaut will make history simply by taking her seat aboard the spacecraft. Christina Koch is set to become the first woman ever to travel beyond low-Earth orbit toward the moon, a milestone moment in human spaceflight.Artemis II is scheduled to launch no earlier than Wednesday, April 1, during a two-hour window opening at 6:24 p.m. EDT, sending four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon and back to Earth. The mission will test the Orion spacecraft’s life-support systems with a crew onboard for the first time as well as navigation and communications technologies essential for future lunar landings.The Apollo program sent 24 male astronauts to the moon between 1968 and 1972, 12 of whom walked on its surface. Koch’s impending journey marks not only a personal achievement but also a symbolic leap forward more than 50 years after NASA’s final moon landing during Apollo 17 in 1972. ForbesComplete Guide To NASA’s Epic Artemis II Mission — Launching This WeekChristina Koch: From Engineer To AstronautKoch, (pronounced “Cook”), a 47-year-old engineer, was selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013. With a background in electrical engineering and physics, Koch spent her early career developing instruments for space missions and working in extreme environments across Antarctica and the Arctic.Before joining NASA, she contributed to major scientific projects at institutions including NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory.She was born in Grand Rapids, Michigan, grew up in Jackson, North Carolina, and now lives in Texas. Christina Koch: Breaking recordsKoch is no stranger to making history. During her first mission in 2019, launching in a Soyuz spacecraft from Kazakhstan, she spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, setting a record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman, surpassing Peggy Whitson’s record. During that mission, she served as a flight engineer on Expeditions 59, 60 and 61, conducting hundreds of experiments and performing six spacewalks. NASA spacewalkers Christina Koch (foreground, suit with red stripe) and Jessica Meir (suit with no stripes) replaced a failed battery charge-discharge unit with a new one during a seven-hour, 17-minute spacewalk.NASA TVChristina Koch: The Historic All-Female SpacewalkAmong Koch’s spacewalks was the first all-female spacewalk, with Jessica Meir, on Oct. 18, 2019.During the seven-hour, 17-minute spacewalk, the astronauts replaced a failed battery charge-discharge unit, a critical component that regulates how solar energy is stored and distributed across the station. The event, a defining moment for women in space exploration, marked Meir’s first spacewalk and Koch’s fourth. Two more all-female spacewalks, both featuring Koch and Meir, followed in January 2020. Christina Koch: On The Shoulders of GiantsKoch’s upcoming mission builds on decades of achievements by pioneering women in space. The first woman to fly in space was Valentina Tereshkova, a Soviet cosmonaut, who launched aboard Vostok 6 on June 16, 1963. She orbited Earth 48 times. A textile factory worker rather than a pilot, Tereshkova was selected in part for her parachuting experience. Although women have historically been underrepresented, with almost 90% of astronauts male, there have been some key milestones:Valentina Tereshkova (1963): First woman in space and only solo female spaceflightSvetlana Savitskaya (1982/1984): First woman on a space station and first female spacewalkerSally Ride (1983): First American woman in spaceMae Jemison (1992): First African American woman in spacePeggy Whitson (2007): First female commander of the International Space StationJessica Meir and Christina Koch (2019): First all-female spacewalkNASA Astronaut Christina Koch answers questions during a postflight news conference at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas on February 12, 2020. (Photo by Mark Felix / AFP) (Photo by MARK FELIX/AFP /AFP via Getty Images)AFP /AFP via Getty ImagesChristina Koch: NASA Artemis II Mission Assigned as mission specialist I on Artemis II, Koch will travel farther from Earth than any woman in history. The mission will take her and her crewmates — Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen — on a 10-day journey around the moon.The mission will include a couple of other historic crew milestones, including the first time a Black man (Glover) and a non-American astronaut (Hansen) travel beyond low-Earth orbit toward the moon.They’ll also travel farther from Earth than any other humans (about 254,600 miles/410,000 kilometers), and their elliptical orbit of the moon takes them 4,600 miles (7,400 kilometers) beyond it. The crew will splash down in the Pacific Ocean off San Diego 10 days after launch.The first crewed lunar flyby of the 21st century is here! Wishing you clear skies and wide eyes.
